passage: The email reached the whole microbiology department at 4 p.m.: Ritu had won the national young scientist fellowship, the one Kalyani had applied for twice and never got. Kalyani read it at her lab bench and felt something tighten in her chest. Four years of teaching Ritu to pipette, to write, to rewrite. Now Ritu's name was bigger than hers. She put the phone face down and cleaned her glassware slowly. Then she walked to the corridor where Ritu stood surrounded by students, looking half-dazed. Kalyani hugged her hard. "This is yours. And a little bit mine too," she said, laughing. That evening she wrote Ritu's name at the top of the lab whiteboard, above her own.

qa.q: How many times had Kalyani applied for the fellowship?
qa.a: Kalyani had applied for it twice and never got it.

qa.q: What did Kalyani feel when she read the email, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt a sting of hurt; her chest tightened and she put the phone face down, cleaning her glassware slowly before she moved.

qa.q: Which choice turned Kalyani's hurt into something good?
qa.a: Walking out to hug Ritu, calling the win partly hers with a laugh, and putting Ritu's name above her own chose pride over rivalry.

qa.q: How might Ritu experience Kalyani's hug in that crowded corridor?
qa.a: She would likely feel deeply relieved and proud 🤍, knowing her mentor is glad for her rather than threatened.

grounding: A woman mentor feels hurt when her mentee wins the fellowship she never got, then chooses pride and celebrates her.

passage:
Subject: Your news 🎉
Dear Vasudha,
I heard this morning that you'll be heading the Chennai design team, the job I once wanted for myself. I'll be honest, because you've always valued that from me: for about an hour I felt a small, silly hurt. You were the shy girl who once asked me, 'Ma'am, how do I name the layers in a file?'
Then I opened your first portfolio, which I still keep, and the hurt turned into something much bigger. Pride. Watching you need me less has been the best result of my work.
Please don't stop calling me, but call me as a friend now, not a student. I'll bring the sweets on Friday.
With so much joy,
Pooja

qa.q: Which team will Vasudha be heading?
qa.a: Vasudha will be heading the Chennai design team.

qa.q: How did Pooja's feelings change after she opened Vasudha's first portfolio?
qa.a: Her brief, small hurt at being passed turned into a much bigger pride in how far Vasudha has come.

qa.q: What makes Pooja's email a mature response to being overtaken?
qa.a: She admits the hurt honestly, chooses pride over rivalry and invites a friendship of equals instead of holding on to the old roles.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel reading that Pooja once wanted this job?
qa.a: She might feel a flicker of guilt at first, then warmth and relief that her mentor is truly glad for her.

grounding: A mentor writes to the mentee who has overtaken her, admitting brief hurt and choosing pride and a friendship of equals.

passage:
People always ask me about the moment Hemant got the grant I had applied for twice and never won. You want the honest answer? For about an hour, it hurt. I'm Elizabeth, the ma'am who trained him when he couldn't even set up a centrifuge, and suddenly he was ahead of me.
I sat in my office and felt this small, mean sting. Then I thought about the first time he ran an experiment alone and phoned me, shouting with joy. I thought, this is what I was doing all those years. So I walked down to his lab and hugged him and said, "You won't need me much now. That's the whole point."
That evening I told my husband it was one of my proudest days.

qa.q: How many times had Elizabeth applied for the grant?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling in her office after hearing the news?
qa.a: She felt a small, mean sting of hurt that Hemant had got ahead of her, before choosing pride.

qa.q: What turning point did Elizabeth choose, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She walked to his lab to celebrate him, seeing his success as part of her own work rather than a rival's win.

qa.q: What might Hemant experience when Elizabeth hugs him?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and deeply valued, knowing his mentor is glad rather than jealous.

grounding: Shows a mentor feeling a flash of hurt when her mentee's success passes hers, then choosing pride over rivalry.

passage:
I sit two desks from Usha, so I saw most of it. When the email came announcing that Ritu, her old trainee, would lead the new regional team, Usha read it twice. She didn't move for a bit. Then she took her glasses off and rubbed her eyes. I couldn't tell what she was feeling.
At lunch she didn't join us. I wondered if she was upset.
But at three o'clock she walked over to Ritu's desk with a small plant from her own window. I heard her say, "You'll be brilliant. Call me if you want, but you won't need to." Ritu went pink. Usha came back to her desk humming. Later I saw her forward the email to her own mentor, with one line: "My student. Look."

qa.q: What did Usha take to Ritu's desk?
qa.a: A small plant from her own window.

qa.q: What might Usha have been feeling when she read the email twice and rubbed her eyes?
qa.a: She may have felt a touch of hurt or surprise at being passed by her former trainee, before deciding to feel proud.

qa.q: Which choice did Usha make after the first moment of hurt, and why did it work?
qa.a: She chose to celebrate Ritu in person and told her she wouldn't need to call, showing gladness at being needed less.

qa.q: What is it like for Ritu when Usha comes over with the plant?
qa.a: Ritu seems moved and a little embarrassed, going pink, and likely relieved that her old mentor is happy for her.

grounding: Shows a colleague's account of a mentor who feels hurt when her trainee is promoted past her, then chooses pride.

passage:
March: Disha's short film, which Anjali had helped her script, was picked for a festival. Anjali's own film had been rejected the same week. She texted "Congrats!!" and then sat in the dark kitchen feeling hollow.
April: Disha asked her to come to the screening. Anjali nearly made an excuse. Instead she went, and watched the audience laugh at a line she had once suggested cutting. She felt a sting, then something warmer.
May: A student asked Anjali who had influenced Disha. Anjali smiled and said, "She did most of it herself. I just got to watch her need me less."

qa.q: What happened to Anjali's own film in March?
qa.a: It was rejected the same week.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling in the dark kitchen in March?
qa.a: She felt hollow and hurt, as Disha's success came the same week as her own rejection.

qa.q: What turning point did Anjali choose in April?
qa.a: Going to the screening instead of making an excuse, which let her move from rivalry to pride.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt when Anjali came to the screening?
qa.a: Disha was probably grateful and relieved to have her mentor there, sharing the moment instead of drifting apart.

grounding: Shows a mentor's hurt when her mentee's film succeeds as hers fails, turning over weeks into pride in being needed less.

passage: Deepa, you want to know about jealousy at work? Let your Ira Maasi confess one. At twenty-six I was a team lead, and I had trained Naveen from his first week: how to write specs, how to handle angry clients. Two years later he won the company's innovation award, the one I had wanted for myself for years. When they called his name, I clapped, and something small and sour turned in my chest. For a whole evening I told myself he had been lucky. Then I remembered his first spec, covered in my red pen, and the night he stayed late to fix it without complaint. The next morning I went to his desk and said, "Your win is partly my work too, and I'm proud of both of us." He grinned and said, "Mostly yours." That's when I learned that the best thing a mentor can feel is less needed.

qa.q: What award did Naveen win?
qa.a: The company's innovation award.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when Naveen's name was called?
qa.a: She felt a small, sour pang of jealousy and hurt while clapping, having wanted that award for years.

qa.q: What turning point did Ira reach the next morning?
qa.a: She chose pride over rivalry, going to Naveen's desk to say his win was partly her work and that she was proud of both of them.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt when Ira came to his desk?
qa.a: Naveen was likely touched and grateful, grinning and giving her credit with 'Mostly yours.'

grounding: Shows a mentor feeling a pang of hurt when a mentee's success passes her own, then choosing pride over rivalry.
